Et abiit, et cœpit prædicare in Decapoli, id est in provincia decem civitates habente.
paras.en: [[5:18|And when he went up into the ship|Quumque ascenderet Jesus navim]], to return to his own country, [[5:18|he that had been troubled with the devil, began to beseech him that he might be with him|cœpit illum deprecari qui a dæmonio vexatus fuerat, et sanatus, ut esset cum illo]], and had been healed; that is, that Jesus would allow him to be and live with him. For he wished to be grateful to Christ for so great a benefit. [[5:19|And he admitted him not|Et non admisit eum]] to be with him, [[5:19|but saith him: Go into thy house to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee|sed ait illi: Vade in domum tuam ad tuos, et annuntia illis quanta tibi Dominus fecerit]]. [[5:20|And he went his way, and began to publish in Decapolis|Et abiit, et cœpit prædicare in Decapoli]], that is, in the province that has ten cities.

paras.t: Præterea recitat Marcus quomodo Christus resuscitavit filiam archisynagogi nomine Jairi, et qualiter eundo ad suscitationem illius curavit in via mulierem a profluvio sanguinis. Utrumque autem miraculum in Matthæo explanatum est.
paras.en: Further, Mark relates how Christ raised the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue named Jairus, and how, going to raise her, he healed on the way the woman with the issue of blood. Both miracles have been explained on Matthew[[Matt 9:18||]].

paras.t: Patet itaque ex Evangelio, quod Christus interdum prohibuit miracula sua publicare, quandoque vero jussit ea manifestari: ad instruendum quod fideles interdum debeant opera sua virtuosa manifestare ad gloriam Dei ædificationemque proximi, ex caritate, prout Paulus sæpissime fecit; interdum vero debent ea occultare, ex humilitate. Denique aliqui dicunt, quod Christus prædictum dæmoniacum non admisit ad suum discipulatum, propter præcedentis passionis horrorem, et ne dæmoni adscriberentur opera quæ faceret virtute Christi exsistendo cum eo: et ob id furiosi ac dæmoniaci, etiam post curationem, in Ecclesia non promoventur.
paras.en: It is plain, then, from the Gospel that Christ sometimes forbade his miracles to be made known[[5:43||]], and sometimes commanded them to be made manifest[[5:19||]]: to teach that the faithful ought sometimes to make their virtuous works known, for the glory of God and the edification of their neighbour, out of charity, as Paul very often did; and sometimes ought to hide them, out of humility. Lastly, some say that Christ did not admit the said demoniac to be his disciple because of the horror of his former affliction, and lest the works he did by Christ's power while living with him should be ascribed to the demon: and for that reason madmen and the possessed, even after they are healed, are not promoted to holy orders in the Church.

6.title: Enarratio capituli sexti: Et egressus inde, abiit in patriam suam
6.title_en: Exposition of the sixth chapter: And going out from thence, he went into his own country

paras.t: Et egressus inde, videlicet a domo archisynagogi, abiit in patriam suam Galilæam. Porro, quod scribitur hic de æmulatione, susurratione et scandalizatione Judæorum propter doctrinam Christi, scriptum et elucidatum est in Matthæo. Ibi enim ostensum est quomodo Marcus dicat dixisse Judæos de Jesu, Nonne hic est faber filius Mariæ? quum Matthæus scribat eos dixisse, Nonne hic est fabri filius? Quod vero hic subditur, Non poterat ibi virtutem, id est operationem miraculosam, ullam facere, etc., intelligendum est de potentia Christi ordinata, quia non decuit propter illorum perversitatem, non de potentia sua absoluta. Et mirabatur propter incredulitatem illorum. Qualiter admiratio locum in Christo habuerit, tractatum est plenius in Matthæo, ubi Salvator legitur propter fidem centurionis fuisse miratus. Quemadmodum vero de illius fide, sic de istorum perfidia mirabatur.
paras.en: [[6:1|And going out from thence|Et egressus inde]], namely from the house of the ruler of the synagogue, [[6:1|he went into his own country|abiit in patriam suam]], Galilee. What is written here of the jealousy, murmuring and scandal of the Jews at Christ's teaching has been written and explained on Matthew[[Matt 13:54||]]. For there it was shown how Mark says the Jews said of Jesus, [[6:3|Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary|Nonne hic est faber filius Mariæ]]?, when Matthew writes that they said, [[Matt 13:55|Is not this the carpenter's son?|Nonne hic est fabri filius?]] And what is added here, [[6:5|And he could not do any miracles there|non poterat ibi virtutem ullam facere]], 'miracles', that is, miraculous working, etc., is to be understood of Christ's ordered power [*potentia ordinata*, his power as it acts according to his own wise ordering], because it was not fitting on account of their perversity, not of his absolute power. [[6:6|And he wondered because of their unbelief|Et mirabatur propter incredulitatem illorum]]. How wonder had place in Christ was treated more fully on Matthew, where the Saviour is read to have wondered at the faith of the centurion[[Matt 8:10||]]. And as he wondered at his faith, so he wondered at their faithlessness.

paras.t: Et circuibat castella in circuitu docens. Nam quamvis ingratos incredulosque compatriotas reliquisset, processit tamen ad eos de quorum informatione spes erat. Et convocavit Jesus duodecim Apostolos, quorum unus fuit Judas Iscariotes, et cœpit eos mittere binos. Quæ autem hic recitantur de missione, prædicatione et miraculis Apostolorum, exposita sunt in Matthæo; ibique concordatum est id in quo Marcus a Matthæo discrepare videtur. Et ungebant Apostoli oleo multos ægros, et sanabantur. Ex hoc elicitur, quod Extrema unctio infirmorum fuit ante passionem instituta a Christo.
paras.en: [[6:6|and he went through the villages round about teaching|Et circuibat castella in circuitu docens]]. For though he had left his ungrateful and unbelieving countrymen, he still went on to those of whose instruction there was hope. [[6:7|And he called the twelve|Et convocavit Jesus duodecim]], Jesus, the twelve Apostles, one of whom was Judas Iscariot, [[6:7|and began to send them two and two|et cœpit eos mittere binos]]. What is related here of the sending, preaching and miracles of the Apostles has been expounded on Matthew[[Matt 10:1||]]; and there was reconciled the point in which Mark seems to differ from Matthew. [[6:13|and anointed with oil many that were sick, and healed them|Et ungebant Apostoli oleo multos ægros, et sanabantur]], the Apostles. From this it is gathered that the Extreme Unction of the sick was instituted by Christ before his passion.

paras.t: Et audivit Herodes rex famam Christi. Manifestum enim factum est nomen ejus, quia non ipse dumtaxat, sed et discipuli ejus signa fecerunt. Et dicebat Herodes: Joannes Baptista resurrexit a mortuis. Scriptura ista continens decollationem Joannis Baptistæ, tota habita atque exposita est in Matthæo.
paras.en: [[6:14|And king Herod heard|Et audivit Herodes rex]] of the fame of Christ. [[6:14|for his name was made manifest|Manifestum enim factum est nomen ejus]], because not only he himself but his disciples too did signs. [[6:14|and he said: John the Baptist is risen again from dead|Et dicebat Herodes: Joannes Baptista resurrexit a mortuis]], Herod. This passage containing the beheading of John the Baptist has been given and expounded in full on Matthew[[Matt 14:1||]].

paras.t: Et convenientes Apostoli ad Jesum, redeuntes videlicet a prædicatione et exsecutione officii eis injuncti, renuntiaverunt ei omnia signa quæ egerant et verba quæ docuerant, submittentes se correctioni atque judicio sui magistri, ostendentes quoque se injunctum negotium fideliter exsecutos. Et ait illis: Venite seorsum in desertum locum, et requiescite pusillum. Pius namque magister ac Dominus discipulorum labori et fatigationi compassus, concessit eis respirationem, recreationem et quietem, verumtamen non magnam nec longam, sed brevem ac modicam: ostendens non diu cessandum esse ab opere bono, nec ultra necessitatem indulgendum esse corporali quieti, sed usque in finem invicto animo perseverandum fore in opere virtuoso. Cur autem abduxerit eos ad locum secretum, subjungitur. Erant enim qui veniebant ad Jesum ejusque Apostolos, et redibant ab eis, multi, sibi invicem in itinere obviantes, et nec manducandi spatium habebant discipuli, propter populorum concursum.
paras.en: [[6:30|And the apostles coming together unto Jesus|Et convenientes Apostoli ad Jesum]], returning, namely, from preaching and carrying out the office laid on them, [[6:30|related to him all things that they had done and taught|renuntiaverunt ei omnia signa quæ egerant et verba quæ docuerant]], all the signs they had done and the words they had taught, submitting themselves to the correction and judgement of their master, and showing that they had faithfully carried out the task given them. [[6:31|And he said to them: Come apart into a desert place, and rest a little|Et ait illis: Venite seorsum in desertum locum, et requiescite pusillum]]. For the kind master and Lord, pitying the labour and weariness of his disciples, granted them a breathing space, refreshment and rest, yet not great nor long but short and slight: showing that one must not cease long from good work, nor indulge bodily rest beyond necessity, but persevere to the end with unconquered mind in virtuous work. Why he led them away to a secluded place is added: [[6:31|For there were many coming and going|Erant enim qui veniebant … et redibant … multi]] to Jesus and his Apostles, meeting one another on the road, [[6:31|and they had not so much as time to eat|et nec manducandi spatium habebant]], the disciples, because of the crowds flocking together.

paras.t: Et ascendentes in navim. Hoc loco Evangelista enarrat miraculum, quemadmodum Christus ex quinque panibus duobusque piscibus saturavit quinque millia hominum, exceptis mulieribus et pueris, ita quod de fragmentis sublati et adimpleti sunt duodecim cophini. Hoc autem miraculum expositum est in Matthæo. Aliquid tamen hic additur, scilicet: Et dixerunt ei, id est discipuli Christo: Euntes emamus ducentis denariis panes, et dabimus eis manducare. Hoc dixerunt ad ostendendum quam impossibile fuerit eis tantam turbam cibare, tanquam dicerent: Quum simus pauperes, non habemus pecuniam sufficientem ad emendum cibaria istis, quia etsi ducentos denarios haberemus, non sufficeret. Unde in evangelio Joannis legitur: Ducentorum denariorum panes non sufficiunt eis, ut unusquisque modicum quid accipiat.
paras.en: [[6:32|And going up into a ship|Et ascendentes in navim]]. Here the Evangelist relates the miracle of how Christ with five loaves and two fishes fed five thousand men, besides women and children, so that twelve baskets were taken up and filled with the fragments. This miracle has been expounded on Matthew[[Matt 14:13||]]. Something, however, is added here, namely: [[6:37|And they said to him|Et dixerunt ei]], that is, the disciples to Christ: [[6:37|Let us go and buy bread for two hundred pence, and we will give them to eat|Euntes emamus ducentis denariis panes, et dabimus eis manducare]]. They said this to show how impossible it was for them to feed so great a crowd, as if to say: since we are poor, we do not have money enough to buy food for these, for even if we had two hundred pence it would not be enough. Hence we read in the Gospel of John: [[John 6:7|Two hundred pennyworth of bread is not sufficient for them that every one may take a little|Ducentorum denariorum panes non sufficiunt eis, ut unusquisque modicum quid accipiat]].

paras.t: Et statim coegit discipulos suos ascendere navim, ut præcederent eum trans fretum ad Bethsaidam, urbem Galilææ, dum ipse dimitteret, id est, a se recedere faceret, populum. Ideo autem dicit Evangelista, quod coegit discipulos suos hoc facere, quia discipuli non libenter navigabant sine eo, imo ubique libenter erant cum eo propter dulcedinem, pietatem et amabilitatem ipsius. Et quum dimisisset eos, id est populum, abiit in montem orare. In quo docuit, quod prædicator verbi Dei, expleto prædicationis et instructionis officio, vitare debet strepitum populi, et ad orationem recurrere atque quieti intendere, ut gratias agat Deo de eo quod bene locutus est, oretque Deum pro auditorum fructu ac salute, et item pro sui ipsius pleniori illustratione, ut habeat semper in promptu quod aliis fructuose proponat.
paras.en: [[6:45|And immediately he obliged his disciples to go up into the ship, that they might go before him over the water to Bethsaida|Et statim coegit discipulos suos ascendere navim, ut præcederent eum trans fretum ad Bethsaidam]], a city of Galilee, [[6:45|whilst he dismissed the people|dum ipse dimitteret populum]], that is, made them go away from him. The Evangelist says he obliged his disciples to do this because the disciples did not gladly sail without him; rather, they were everywhere glad to be with him because of his sweetness, kindness and lovableness. [[6:46|And when he had dismissed them|Et quum dimisisset eos]], that is, the people, [[6:46|he went up to the mountain to pray|abiit in montem orare]]. By this he taught that the preacher of the word of God, having fulfilled the office of preaching and instruction, should avoid the noise of the people and return to prayer and give himself to quiet, so as to thank God for having spoken well, and pray God for the fruit and salvation of his hearers, and also for his own fuller enlightenment, so as always to have ready something to set fruitfully before others.

paras.t: Et quum sero esset. Quidquid in isto capitulo subditur de ambulatione Domini Jesu supra mare et discipulorum conturbatione, de miraculis quoque Christi factis in terra Genesareth, dictum et declaratum est in Matthæo, paucis demptis, quæ exponenda sunt jam. Et volebat Jesus ambulans supra mare, præterire eos, puta discipulos in navi periclitantes. Forte sic voluit eos præterire, quomodo post resurrectionem finxit se longius ire. Nec fuit aliqua simulatio, duplicitas sive deceptio, quoniam ad designandum aliquid spirituale hoc egit, videlicet propter ostendendam imperfectionem fidei discipulorum suorum, ob quam fuit quodammodo spiritualiter elongatus ab eis. In plateis ponebant infirmos. Quidam Sanctorum dicunt Petrum fecisse majora signa quam fecerit Christus, ut Christus prædixit apud Joannem: Qui credit in me, opera quæ ego facio et ipse faciet, et majora horum faciet, quia ego ad Patrem vado. In hoc autem asserunt Petrum fecisse majora, quia de eo scriptum est in Actibus: In plateis ejiciebant infirmos, ut veniente Petro, saltem umbra illius obumbraret quemquam illorum, et liberarentur ab infirmitate sua. Et dicunt quod hoc nusquam legitur de Christo. Quibus obviare videtur quod hoc loco recitat Marcus: Quocumque introibat, in vicos, vel in villas, aut in civitates, in plateis ponebant infirmos. Sed qui dictum illorum cupit tueri, dicere potest quod Evangelista non ait aliquem languidorum sola obumbratione corporis Christi fuisse sanatum, sed tactu.
paras.en: [[6:47|And when it was late|Et quum sero esset]]. Whatever is added in this chapter about the Lord Jesus walking on the sea and the disciples' alarm, and about Christ's miracles done in the land of Genesareth, has been said and explained on Matthew[[Matt 14:23||]], except for a few things which are now to be expounded. [[6:48|he cometh to them walking upon the sea, and he would have passed by them|ambulans supra mare, præterire eos]], namely the disciples in danger in the ship. Perhaps he wished to pass them by in the way that after the resurrection [[Luke 24:28|he made as though he would go farther|finxit se longius ire]]. Nor was there any pretence, doubleness or deceit, since he did this to signify something spiritual, namely to show the imperfection of his disciples' faith, because of which he was in a manner spiritually far from them. [[6:56|they laid the sick in the streets|in plateis ponebant infirmos]]. Some of the Saints say that Peter did greater signs than Christ did, as Christ foretold in John: [[John 14:12|he that believeth in me, the works that I do, he also shall do: and greater than these shall he do|Qui credit in me, opera quæ ego facio et ipse faciet, et majora horum faciet]], because I go to the Father. And they assert that Peter did greater things in this, that it is written of him in the Acts: [[Acts 5:15|they brought forth the sick into the streets|In plateis ejiciebant infirmos]], [[Acts 5:15|that, when Peter came, his shadow at the least might overshadow any of them and they might be delivered from their infirmities|ut veniente Petro, saltem umbra illius obumbraret quemquam illorum, et liberarentur ab infirmitate sua]]. And they say this is nowhere read of Christ. What Mark relates in this place seems to stand against them: [[6:56|And whithersoever he entered, into towns or into villages or cities, they laid the sick in the streets|Quocumque introibat, in vicos, vel in villas, aut in civitates, in plateis ponebant infirmos]]. But whoever wishes to defend their saying can say that the Evangelist does not say that any of the sick was healed by the mere shadow of Christ's body, but by touch.

7.title: Expositio capituli septimi: Et conveniunt ad eum pharisæi et quidam de scribis
7.title_en: Exposition of the seventh chapter: “And there assembled together unto him the Pharisees and some of the scribes”

paras.t: Consequenter Evangelista describit invidiosam increpationem Scribarum ac Pharisæorum, increpantium Salvatorem eo quod discipuli manducabant manibus communibus, id est non lotis, justamque redargutionem eorum a Christo: et quod hic induci possit pro expositione, introductum est in Matthæo, ubi scriptura ista exposita est, perpaucis exceptis, quæ modo tangenda sunt. Et a foro nisi baptizentur, id est, Scribæ, Pharisæi, ceterique Judæi redeuntes a foro seu loco extraneo, nisi lavent se, non comedunt. Et alia multa sunt quæ tradita sunt illis servare, videlicet, baptismata, id est lotiones, calicum et urceorum.
paras.en: Next the Evangelist describes the envious rebuke of the Scribes and Pharisees, who rebuked the Saviour because His disciples ate [[7:2|with common, that is, with unwashed hands|manibus communibus, id est non lotis]], and Christ's just reproof of them; and whatever could be brought in here by way of exposition has been brought in on Matthew[[Matt 15:1||]], where this passage is explained, with very few exceptions, which are now to be touched on. [[7:4|And when they come from the market, unless they be washed|Et a foro nisi baptizentur]], that is, the Scribes, the Pharisees and the rest of the Jews, coming back from the market or from some place outside, unless they wash themselves, [[7:4|they eat not|non comedunt]]. [[7:4|and many other things there are that have been delivered to them to observe|Et alia multa sunt quæ tradita sunt illis servare]], namely, [[7:4|the washings|baptismata]], that is, the cleansings, [[7:4|of cups and of pots|calicum et urceorum]].

paras.t: Omne extrinsecus introiens in hominem, id est alimentum corporale, non potest eum coinquinare, id est hominem maculare, seu peccatoribus similem facere, quantum est ex natura vel parte alimenti, quia omnis creatura Dei bona est. Et in secessum exit, purgans materialiter omnes escas nutritivas, quæ in substantiam aliti convertuntur. Per hoc enim quod natura egerit superfluum alimenti, id quod remanet purificatur, separato superfluo et immundo a mundo et necessario.
paras.en: [[7:18|every thing from without entering into a man|Omne extrinsecus introiens in hominem]], that is, bodily food, [[7:18|cannot defile him|non potest eum coinquinare]], that is, stain the man, or make him like to sinners, so far as the nature or the part of the food is concerned, because [[1 Tim 4:4|every creature of God is good|omnis creatura Dei bona est]]. [[7:19|and goeth out into the privy|Et in secessum exit]], [[7:19|purging|purgans]] materially [[7:19|all meats|omnes escas]] that nourish, which are turned into the substance of the one who is fed. For by nature's casting out what is superfluous in the food, what remains is purified, the superfluous and unclean being separated from the clean and necessary.

paras.t: Et ingressus Jesus domum, neminem extraneorum voluit scire: id est, quantum in se fuit, occultavit se, et non permisit ut discipuli sui se manifestarent, docens fugere ostentationem inanem, ut amemus nesciri. Et non potuit latere, secundum naturalem cursum et ordinem, propter celebrem famam ipsius. Nam et honor sequitur fugientem, et non potest civitas abscondi posita supra montem. Loquendo autem de absoluta Christi potentia, certum est quod latere potuerit, imo et se invisibilem reddere, etiam stando inter alios.
paras.en: [[7:24|And entering into a house, he would that no man should know it|Et ingressus Jesus domum, neminem extraneorum voluit scire]] (no man, that is, from outside): that is, as far as lay in Him, He hid Himself, and did not allow His disciples to make Him known, teaching us to shun empty display, so that we may love to be unknown. [[7:24|And he could not be hid|Et non potuit latere]], according to the natural course and order of things, because of His great fame. For honour follows the man who flees it, and [[Matt 5:14|a city seated on a mountain cannot be hid|non potest civitas abscondi posita supra montem]]. But speaking of Christ's absolute power, it is certain that He could have been hid, and even have made Himself invisible while standing among others.

paras.t: Mulier enim statim, etc. Hic describitur curatio filiæ mulieris gentilis, Syrophœnissæ genere, id est natæ de Syria Phœnicis: estque locus iste expositus in Matthæo.
paras.en: [[7:25|For a woman as soon as|Mulier enim statim]], etc. Here is described the healing of the daughter of a gentile woman, [[7:26|a Syrophenician born|Syrophœnissæ genere]], that is, born in Syrian Phœnicia; and this passage has been explained on Matthew[[Matt 15:21||]].

paras.t: Et iterum exiens Jesus de finibus Tyri, venit per Sidonem ad mare Galilææ, inter medios fines Decapoleos, id est regionis quæ vocatur Decapolis, quasi decem civitates habens. Et adducunt ei turbæ surdum et mutum, et deprecabantur eum ut imponat illi manum. Iste surdus et mutus, ut dicitur, factus fuit talis a dæmone ipsum possidente, qui usum linguæ et aurium impedivit in eo. Unde in Matthæo legitur: Tunc oblatus est dæmonium habens, cæcus et mutus.
paras.en: [[7:31|And again going out of the coasts of Tyre, he came by Sidon to the sea of Galilee|Et iterum exiens Jesus de finibus Tyri, venit per Sidonem ad mare Galilææ]], in the midst of [[7:31|the coasts of Decapolis|fines Decapoleos]], that is, of the region called Decapolis, as having ten cities. [[7:32|And they bring to him one deaf and dumb: and they besought him that he would lay his hand upon him|Et adducunt ei turbæ surdum et mutum, et deprecabantur eum ut imponat illi manum]]. This deaf and dumb man, so it is said, had been made so by the demon possessing him, which hindered in him the use of tongue and ears. Hence we read in Matthew: [[Matt 12:22|Then was offered to him one possessed with a devil, blind and dumb|Tunc oblatus est dæmonium habens, cæcus et mutus]].

paras.t: Et apprehendens Jesus eum surdum et mutum, de turba seorsum, ex humilitate, vel quoniam turba digna non erat videre mysterium hujus miraculi, vel ad designandum quod spiritualiter surdi ac muti secrete admonendi sunt atque docendi, ne ex humano rubore retrahantur ab advertentia et pœnitentia; misit digitos suos in auriculas ejus: primo, ad ostendendum quod divinitas in eo latens operabatur per corpus assumptum, tanquam per instrumentum animatum, conjunctum ac proprium, quemadmodum anima rationalis operatur per corpus a se informatum; secundo, quia per digitos, ratione articulationis et distinctionis ipsorum, significatur discretio: ad aperiendum autem aures interiores hominis spiritualiter surdi, discretio magna exigitur. Et exspuens, tetigit suo sputo linguam ejus: quia per salivam, sine qua verba formari non possunt perfecte, sapientia figuratur, sine qua nemo rationabiliter loquitur. Exspuit ergo, et tetigit Jesus linguam surdi ac muti, ad insinuandum quod qui mutus est a prolatione verborum cælestium atque salubrium, recte ac meritorie loqui non potest, nisi divina sapientia perfundatur. Propter quod orat Apostolus, ut detur sibi sapientia in apertione oris sui.
paras.en: [[7:33|And taking him|Et apprehendens Jesus eum]], the deaf and dumb man, [[7:33|from the multitude apart|de turba seorsum]]: out of humility; or because the crowd was not worthy to see the mystery of this miracle; or to signify that the spiritually deaf and dumb are to be admonished and taught in secret, lest human shame hold them back from heeding and doing penance; [[7:33|he put his fingers into his ears|misit digitos suos in auriculas ejus]]: first, to show that the Godhead hidden in Him worked through the body He had taken, as through a living instrument joined to it and its own, just as the rational soul works through the body which it informs; secondly, because the fingers, being jointed and distinct from one another, signify discretion: and to open the inner ears of a man spiritually deaf, great discretion is required. [[7:33|And spitting, he touched his tongue|Et exspuens, tetigit suo sputo linguam ejus]] with His spittle: because saliva, without which words cannot be perfectly formed, figures wisdom, without which no one speaks reasonably. So Jesus spat and touched the tongue of the deaf and dumb man, to suggest that one who is dumb as to uttering heavenly and wholesome words cannot speak rightly and meritoriously unless he is filled with divine wisdom. For this reason the Apostle prays that wisdom may be given him in the opening of his mouth[[Eph 6:19||]].

paras.t: Et suspiciens in cælum, ad demonstrandum quod tota virtus sua esset a Patre, et quod ab eo auxilium habuerit secundum quod homo, ingemuit. Quare ingemuit? Numquid propter difficultatem perpetrandi miraculi? Non utique: sed ex compassione qua non solum præsenti infirmo, sed universis condoluit, qui dæmonum dominatione premuntur; et item, ad ostendendum quam difficile sanaretur anima spiritualiter surda ac muta. Unde in suscitatione Lazari turbavit se ipsum, fremens spiritu, et lacrimas fundens, ad demonstrandum quod mole consuetudinis impiæ pressi obstinati, super quos clausit puteus os suum, qui figurantur per quatriduanum mortuum, difficillime convertuntur et vitam gratiæ sortiuntur. Et ait Jesus illi surdo et muto, Ephphetha, quod est, adaperire. Et statim apertæ sunt aures ejus, id est ad audiendum aptatæ, et naturali usui redditæ, et solutum est vinculum, id est impedimentum, linguæ ejus, et loquebatur recte. Sic qui spiritualis visus illustrationem interiorumque aurium apertionem a Christo sortitur, loquitur recte, id est juste, sapienter atque salubriter, prout monet Apostolus: Sermo vester semper in gratia sale sit conditus.
paras.en: [[7:34|And looking up to heaven|Et suspiciens in cælum]], to show that all His power was from the Father, and that He had help from Him as man, [[7:34|he groaned|ingemuit]]. Why did He groan? Was it because of the difficulty of working the miracle? Certainly not: but out of compassion, by which He grieved not only for the sick man before Him but for all who are oppressed by the dominion of demons; and also to show how hard it is for a soul spiritually deaf and dumb to be healed. So at the raising of Lazarus He [[John 11:33|troubled himself|turbavit se ipsum]], groaning in spirit[[John 11:38||]] and shedding tears[[John 11:35||]], to show that the obstinate, pressed down by the weight of wicked habit, over whom the pit has shut its mouth[[Ps 68:16||]] [the margin as read gives Ps. vxvut, 46; the words recall Ps 68:16, “let not the pit shut her mouth upon me”], and who are figured by the man four days dead[[John 11:39||]], are converted with the greatest difficulty and come to the life of grace. And Jesus [[7:34|said to him|ait Jesus illi]], the deaf and dumb man: [[7:34|Ephpheta, which is, Be thou opened|Ephphetha, quod est, adaperire]]. [[7:35|And immediately his ears were opened|Et statim apertæ sunt aures ejus]], that is, made fit for hearing and restored to their natural use, [[7:35|and the string|et solutum est vinculum]], that is, the impediment, [[7:35|of his tongue was loosed|linguæ ejus]], [[7:35|and he spoke right|et loquebatur recte]]. So he who receives from Christ the enlightening of spiritual sight and the opening of the inner ears speaks right, that is, justly, wisely and wholesomely, as the Apostle admonishes: [[Col 4:6|Let your speech be always in grace seasoned with salt|Sermo vester semper in gratia sale sit conditus]].

paras.t: Et præcepit illis, id est turbæ, ne cui dicerent, id est, nulli revelarent curationem hanc miraculosam. Quanto autem eis præcipiebat tacere, tanto plus prædicabant. Non tamen rebelles fuerunt, quia utrumque bonum fuit secundum considerationes diversas, et præceptum Salvatoris intelligendum erat, ne ad jactantiam diceretur. Et eo amplius admirabantur, dicentes: Bene omnia fecit. De quibus omnibus subditur: et surdos fecit audire, et mutos loqui. Quamvis enim Marcus non exprimat hic nisi de cura unius, tamen quando Christus istum curavit, sanavit et alios multos surdos et mutos, ac cæcos et debiles, ut habetur in Matthæo. Sed Marcus scribit de uno cujus curatio solennius facta est, et multa mystica figuravit: eratque mirabilior, quia in uno homine tria signa simul facta videntur, dum obsessus liberatur, surdus auditum, et mutus loquelam recuperat. Non tamen certus sum an iste surdus et mutus sit idem de quo scribit Matthæus, asserens eum obsessum a dæmone.
paras.en: [[7:36|And he charged them|Et præcepit illis]], that is, the crowd, [[7:36|that they should tell no man|ne cui dicerent]], that is, that they should reveal this miraculous healing to no one. [[7:36|But the more he charged them|Quanto autem eis præcipiebat]] to be silent, [[7:36|so much the more a great deal did they publish it|tanto plus prædicabant]]. Yet they were not rebellious, because both were good, under different considerations; and the Saviour's command was to be understood as forbidding them to speak of it for boasting. [[7:37|And so much the more did they wonder, saying: He hath done all things well.|Et eo amplius admirabantur, dicentes: Bene omnia fecit.]] Of all of which it is added: [[7:37|He hath made both the deaf to hear and the dumb to speak|et surdos fecit audire, et mutos loqui]]. For although Mark here speaks expressly only of the cure of one man, yet when Christ cured him He also healed many others, deaf and dumb, blind and feeble, as we have in Matthew[[Matt 15:30||]]. But Mark writes of one whose cure was done with more solemnity and figured many mysteries; and it was the more wonderful because in one man three signs are seen to be done at once: the possessed is set free, the deaf recovers hearing, and the dumb speech. Yet I am not certain whether this deaf and dumb man is the same of whom Matthew writes, asserting that he was possessed by a demon.

8.title: Elucidatio capituli octavi: In diebus illis, iterum quum multa turba esset cum Jesu
8.title_en: Explanation of the eighth chapter: In those days again, when there was a great multitude with Jesus

paras.t: In diebus illis, etc. Hoc loco Marcus describit quemadmodum Christus ex septem panibus et paucis pisciculis satiavit quatuor millia hominum, ita quod septem sublatæ sunt sportæ fragmentorum: et istud expositum est in Matthæo.
paras.en: [[8:1|In those days again|In diebus illis]], etc. Here Mark describes how Christ with seven loaves and a few little fishes fed four thousand men, so that seven baskets of fragments were taken up: and this has been expounded on Matthew[[Matt 15:32||]].

paras.t: Et statim ascendens navim cum discipulis suis, venit in partes Dalmanutha. In Matthæo habetur: In fines Magedan. Locus enim binomius fuit, secundum quosdam. Et exierunt Pharisæi, quærentes signum de cœlo. Et ingemiscens spiritu, id est, cordialiter illorum cæcitati et perversitati compatiens Jesus, et dimittens illos, tanquam incorrigibiles, præcipiebat discipulis, dicens: Cavete a fermento, id est doctrina, Pharisæorum, et a fermento Herodis, id est a secta atque malitia Herodianorum, de quibus præhabitum est. Cetera hic omissa patent ex his quæ dicta sunt in Matthæo, ubi omnia ista multo plenius quam in hoc capitulo describuntur.
paras.en: [[8:10|And immediately going up into a ship with his disciples, he came into the parts of Dalmanutha|Et statim ascendens navim cum discipulis suis, venit in partes Dalmanutha]]. In Matthew we have: [[Matt 15:39|into the coasts of Magedan|In fines Magedan]]. For the place had two names, according to some. [[8:11|And the Pharisees came forth|Et exierunt Pharisæi]], [[8:11|asking him a sign from heaven|quærentes signum de cœlo]]. [[8:12|And sighing deeply in spirit|Et ingemiscens spiritu]], that is, Jesus grieving from his heart over their blindness and perversity, and dismissing them as incorrigible, [[8:15|he charged them saying: Take heed and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees|præcipiebat … dicens: Cavete a fermento … Pharisæorum]], his disciples; 'leaven', that is, teaching; [[8:15|and of the leaven of Herod|et a fermento Herodis]], that is, from the sect and malice of the Herodians, of whom we have spoken before. The rest, left out here, is plain from what was said on Matthew[[Matt 16:1||]], where all this is described much more fully than in this chapter.

paras.t: Et veniunt Bethsaidam; et adducunt ei cæcum, et rogabant eum ut illum cæcum tangeret, scientes quod tangendo eum illuminaret. Isti adducentes cæcum, videntur fuisse turbæ, non discipuli. Et apprehensa manu cæci, eduxit eum extra vicum, in quo fuit sibi adductus, ad demonstrandum quod eum qui divinitus illustrari desiderat, necesse est pristinos actus relinquere, imo se ipsum abnegare, et quasi de terrenis ad cœlestia transmeare. Et exspuens in oculos ejus, ad ostendendum quod interiorum oculorum illustratio sit per immissionem sapientiæ profluentis a Christo. Per salivam nempe sapientia designatur. Vel ideo exspuit in oculos ejus, ut potestatem suam ostenderet, quando et per contactum sputi sui cæcus reciperet visum. Impositis manibus suis super cæcum, et forte super oculos ejus, interrogavit eum, non quasi ignorans, si aliquid videret. Et adspiciens, ait, id est, cæcus iste videre incipiens et obscure illuminatus, respondit: Video homines quasi arbores ambulantes, id est, corpora video moveri, sed distinctionem membrorum et figuras lineamentorum non discerno in eis. Deinde iterum imposuit Jesus manus super oculos ejus, et cœpit videre, et restitutus est, id est, ad usum oculorum reductus est, ita ut clare videret omnia colorata seu lucida sibi objecta. Per impositionem manuum Salvatoris, designatur applicatio suæ divinæ virtutis, qua hominem illustrante, videt clare omnia ad veram salutem spectantia.
paras.en: [[8:22|And they came to Bethsaida: and they bring to him a blind man. And they besought him that he would touch him|Et veniunt Bethsaidam; et adducunt ei cæcum, et rogabant eum ut illum cæcum tangeret]], knowing that by touching him he would give him light. Those who brought the blind man seem to have been the crowds, not the disciples. [[8:23|And taking the blind man by the hand, he led him out of the town|Et apprehensa manu cæci, eduxit eum extra vicum]] in which he had been brought to him, to show that whoever desires to be enlightened by God must leave his former acts, nay deny himself, and pass as it were from earthly to heavenly things. [[8:23|And spitting upon his eyes|Et exspuens in oculos ejus]], to show that the enlightening of the inward eyes is by the sending in of the wisdom that flows from Christ; for by spittle wisdom is signified. Or he spat on his eyes to show his power, when even by the touch of his spittle the blind man received his sight. [[8:23|laying his hands on him|Impositis manibus suis super cæcum]], and perhaps on his eyes, [[8:23|he asked him if he saw any thing|interrogavit eum, non quasi ignorans, si aliquid videret]], not as one who did not know. [[8:24|And looking up, he said|Et adspiciens, ait]], that is, this blind man, beginning to see and dimly enlightened, answered: [[8:24|I see men, as it were trees, walking|Video homines quasi arbores ambulantes]], that is, I see bodies moving, but I do not make out in them the distinction of limbs or the shapes of their features. [[8:25|After that again he laid his hands upon his eyes: and he began to see and was restored|Deinde iterum imposuit Jesus manus super oculos ejus, et cœpit videre, et restitutus est]], Jesus; restored, that is, brought back to the use of his eyes, [[8:25|so that he saw all things clearly|ita ut clare videret omnia]], all coloured or bright things set before him. By the laying on of the Saviour's hands the application of his divine power is signified, by which, when it enlightens a man, he sees clearly all that concerns true salvation.

paras.t: Sed cur Christus omnipotens curavit hunc cæcum successive, quem poterat in instanti perfecte curare? Dicendum quod primo, ad ostendendum quod homo paulatim crescit et proficit in gratia, ita quod purgatio præcedit illuminationem, illuminatio quoque perfectionem seu unionem. Secundo, ad ostendendum imperfectionem fidei, tam cæci istius, quam turbæ ac discipulorum. Quemadmodum enim Prophetæ interdum verbis, interdum signis et factis prophetaverunt; sic Christus aliquando verbis, aliquando factis aliquid designavit aut præmonstravit, ut quum maledixit ficulneam. Sic igitur in præsenti paulatim illuminavit hunc cæcum, significans homines istos obscuram fidem habere, et clariori lumine indigere.
paras.en: But why did the almighty Christ heal this blind man by stages, when he could have healed him perfectly in an instant? It must be said: first, to show that man grows and advances in grace little by little, so that purgation goes before illumination, and illumination before perfection, or union [the three ways of the spiritual life]. Secondly, to show the imperfection of faith, both of this blind man and of the crowd and the disciples. For as the Prophets prophesied sometimes by words, sometimes by signs and deeds, so Christ sometimes by words, sometimes by deeds signified or showed something beforehand, as when he cursed the fig tree[[Matt 21:19||]]. So here he enlightened this blind man little by little, signifying that these men had a dim faith and needed a clearer light.

paras.t: Præterea S. Marcus describit quomodo Christus interrogavit discipulos suos quid homines de ipso sentirent, seu quem eum esse assererent, et quomodo suam passionem palam prædixit, et Petrum oppositum persuadentem dire redarguit, omnes quoque qui aderant, ad suæ passionis imitationem et adversitatum tolerantiam admonebat. Quæ omnia habita atque exposita sunt in Matthæo.
paras.en: Further, St Mark describes how Christ asked his disciples what men thought of him, or whom they asserted him to be, and how he openly foretold his passion, and sternly rebuked Peter for urging the opposite, and admonished all who were present to imitate his passion and bear adversities. All of which has been given and expounded on Matthew[[Matt 16:13||]].

paras.t: Aliqua tamen adduntur vel variantur quantum ad verba, quia hic dicitur: Qui enim me confusus fuerit, et verba mea. Pro quo in Luca habetur: Qui me erubuerit et meos sermones. Et est sensus: Qui turpe æstimat ut a me christianus vocetur, et me esse Filium Dei confiteri non audet, meaque verba observare confunditur. In generatione ista adultera et peccatrice, id est inter homines spiritualiter fornicantes recedendo a Deo vero et rebus caducis inhærendo: de quibus fertur in Psalmo, Perdidisti omnes qui fornicantur abs te; et in Osee, Fornicati (inquit) sunt a Deo suo. Deus enim est sponsus animarum, qui primo desponsavit sibi Synagogam in datione legis, deinde Ecclesiam. Et Filius hominis confundetur eum, id est, per modum erubescentis se habebit quantum ad ipsum, non confitendo eum pertinere ad se, neque ad numerum electorum, quum venerit in gloria Patris sui, ad quam in ascensione conscendit: et nunc advocatus eorum est qui ipsum non erubescunt in sæculo isto.
paras.en: Some things, however, are added or varied as to the words, since here it is said: [[8:38|For he that shall be ashamed of me and of my words|Qui enim me confusus fuerit, et verba mea]]. For which in Luke we have: [[Luke 9:26|he that shall be ashamed of me and of my words|Qui me erubuerit et meos sermones]] [Mark's Latin has *confusus fuerit*, 'shall be confounded by me'; Luke's *erubuerit*, 'shall blush for me']. And the sense is: whoever thinks it shameful to be called a Christian after me, and dares not confess that I am the Son of God, and is ashamed to keep my words, [[8:38|in this adulterous and sinful generation|In generatione ista adultera et peccatrice]], that is, among men who commit spiritual fornication by departing from the true God and clinging to perishable things: of whom it is said in the Psalm, [[Ps 72:27|thou hast destroyed all them that are disloyal to thee|Perdidisti omnes qui fornicantur abs te]] [the Latin has 'who commit fornication against thee']; and in Osee: [[Osee 4:12|they have committed fornication against their God|Fornicati (inquit) sunt a Deo suo]]. For God is the bridegroom of souls, who first espoused the Synagogue to himself in the giving of the law, and then the Church. [[8:38|the Son of man also will be ashamed of him|Et Filius hominis confundetur eum]], that is, will behave towards him as one ashamed, not confessing that he belongs to him or to the number of the elect, [[8:38|when he shall come in the glory of his Father|quum venerit in gloria Patris sui]], to which he ascended at the ascension: and he is now the advocate of those who are not ashamed of him in this world.

10.title: Explanatio capituli decimi: Et inde exsurgens, venit in fines Judææ
10.title_en: Explanation of the tenth chapter: “And rising up from thence, he cometh into the coasts of Judea”

paras.t: Hoc loco S. Marcus describit quemadmodum Pharisæi animo tentandi sciscitabantur a Christo, an liceret marito uxorem dimittere: patetque intellectus hujus scripturæ ex his quæ in Matthæo dicta sunt, quamvis ordo verborum et modus loquendi hic et ibi parum mutetur. Hic enim habetur, quod Christus interrogavit Pharisæos: Quid vobis præcepit Moyses? Qui dixerunt: Moyses permisit libellum repudii scribere. Ibi vero habetur, quod Pharisæi interrogaverunt a Christo: Cur Moyses mandavit dare libellum repudii? Ad quod dici potest, quod Christus primo interrogavit eos, ut recitat Marcus; quumque Salvator dixisset verbum Moysis non esse intelligendum ut ipsi putabant, petierunt a Christo, cur Moyses illud mandasset seu permisisset.
paras.en: In this place St Mark describes how the Pharisees, in a spirit of tempting, inquired of Christ whether it was lawful for a husband to put away his wife; and the meaning of this passage is plain from what was said on Matthew[[Matt 19:1||]], although the order of the words and the manner of speaking are a little changed here and there. For here we have that Christ asked the Pharisees: [[10:3|What did Moses command you?|Quid vobis præcepit Moyses?]] [[10:4|Who said: Moses permitted to write a bill of divorce|Qui dixerunt: Moyses permisit libellum repudii scribere]]. There, however, we have that the Pharisees asked Christ: [[Matt 19:7|Why then did Moses command to give a bill of divorce|Cur Moyses mandavit dare libellum repudii]]? To which it may be said that Christ first questioned them, as Mark relates; and when the Saviour had said that the word of Moses was not to be understood as they thought, they asked Christ why Moses had commanded or permitted it.

paras.t: Quisquis non receperit, id est recipere seu adipisci studuerit, regnum Dei, id est patriam Beatorum, velut parvulus, id est in vera humilitate exsistens, et parvulorum innocentiam sequens, non intrabit in illud post vitam præsentem. Idcirco per Salomonem Sapientia ait: Si quis est parvulus, veniat ad me. Et complexans eos, id est, Jesus parvulos sibi præsentatos amplectens, et imponens manus super illos, benedicebat eos. In quo patet quantum Salvator dilexit humanam naturam, dummodo innocentia adornetur.
paras.en: [[10:15|whosoever shall not receive|Quisquis non receperit]], that is, shall not strive to receive or obtain, [[10:15|the kingdom of God|regnum Dei]], that is, the fatherland of the Blessed, [[10:15|as a little child|velut parvulus]], that is, standing in true humility and following the innocence of little children, [[10:15|shall not enter into it|non intrabit in illud]] after the present life. Therefore Wisdom says through Solomon: [[Prov 9:4|Whosoever is a little one, let him come to me.|Si quis est parvulus, veniat ad me.]] [[10:16|And embracing them|Et complexans eos]], that is, Jesus embracing the little ones presented to Him, [[10:16|and laying his hands upon them, he blessed them|et imponens manus super illos, benedicebat eos]]. In this it is plain how much the Saviour loved human nature, provided it is adorned with innocence.

paras.t: Præterea Evangelista commemorat, quemadmodum quidam adolescens ac dives petivit a Christo, Magister bone, quid faciam ut vitam æternam percipiam? et quomodo Christus ei respondit, atque adversus avaritiam disputavit. Quæ omnia in Matthæo exposita sunt.
paras.en: Further, the Evangelist relates how a certain young man, and a rich one, asked of Christ: [[10:17|Good Master, what shall I do that I may receive life everlasting?|Magister bone, quid faciam ut vitam æternam percipiam?]] and how Christ answered him, and spoke against avarice. All of this has been explained on Matthew[[Matt 19:16||]].

paras.t: Et cœpit Petrus ei dicere: Ecce nos dimisimus omnia, et secuti sumus te. Locus iste in Matthæo expositus est. Aliquid tamen hic variatur quantum ad verba. Pauca verba adduntur, quum dicitur: Respondens Jesus, ait: Amen dico vobis, nemo est qui reliquerit domum, aut fratres, aut sorores, etc., propter me et Evangelium, id est, ut evangelicam observet doctrinam, qui non accipiat centies tantum nunc in tempore hoc, domos, et fratres, et sorores. Pro quo Matthæus scripsit: Centuplum accipiet. Quod in Matthæo expositum recolo. Non enim intelligendum est carnaliter, ut millenarii æstimabant, quasi talis pro uno patre habiturus sit in hoc sæculo centum patres, et pro una matre ac conjuge, centum matres atque uxores; sed accipiet talia centies multiplicata æquivalenter, et in potioribus bonis, id est, spiritualia bona, gratiam, virtutes, dona et fructus Spiritus Sancti in hoc sæculo obtinebit. Cum persecutionibus: quia per multas tribulationes oportet nos ingredi regnum cælorum. Sed quomodo persecutiones assignantur inter præmia, quum potius spectent ad merita? nisi quod donum Dei est et beneficium magnum, pati pro Christo adversa, quemadmodum dicit Apostolus: Vobis datum est pro Christo, non solum ut credatis in eum, verum etiam ut patiamini pro illo.
paras.en: [[10:28|And Peter began to say unto him: Behold, we have left all things and have followed thee.|Et cœpit Petrus ei dicere: Ecce nos dimisimus omnia, et secuti sumus te.]] This passage has been explained on Matthew[[Matt 19:27||]]. Yet something is varied here as to the words. A few words are added, when it is said: [[10:29|Jesus answering said: Amen I say to you, there is no man who hath left house or brethren or sisters|Respondens Jesus, ait: Amen dico vobis, nemo est qui reliquerit domum, aut fratres, aut sorores]], etc., [[10:29|for my sake and for the gospel|propter me et Evangelium]], that is, in order to keep the teaching of the Gospel, [[10:30|Who shall not receive an hundred times as much, now in this time: houses and brethren and sisters|qui non accipiat centies tantum nunc in tempore hoc, domos, et fratres, et sorores]]. For which Matthew wrote: [[Matt 19:29|shall receive an hundredfold|Centuplum accipiet]]. This I remember explaining on Matthew. For it is not to be understood carnally, as the millenarians supposed, as though such a man were to have in this world a hundred fathers for one father, and for one mother and one wife a hundred mothers and wives; but he will receive such things multiplied a hundredfold by equivalence, and in better goods: that is, he will obtain in this world spiritual goods, grace, the virtues, and the gifts and fruits of the Holy Ghost. [[10:30|with persecutions|Cum persecutionibus]]: because [[Acts 14:21|through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God|per multas tribulationes oportet nos ingredi regnum cælorum]]. But how are persecutions counted among the rewards, when they belong rather to merits? Only because it is a gift of God and a great benefit to suffer adversity for Christ, as the Apostle says: [[Phil 1:29|For unto you it is given for Christ, not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for him|Vobis datum est pro Christo, non solum ut credatis in eum, verum etiam ut patiamini pro illo]].

paras.t: Erant autem in via ascendentes Jerosolymam, et præcedebat illos Jesus. Et stupebant, hoc est, in doctrina Christi mirabantur, ut patet in textu; et sequentes discipuli Jesum, timebant, propter difficultatem implendi verba Christi. Dicebant enim: Quis poterit salvus fieri?
paras.en: [[10:32|And they were in the way going up to Jerusalem: and Jesus went before them.|Erant autem in via ascendentes Jerosolymam, et præcedebat illos Jesus.]] [[10:32|And they were astonished|Et stupebant]], that is, they wondered at the teaching of Christ, as is plain from the text[[10:24||]]; [[10:32|and following|et sequentes]], the disciples following Jesus, [[10:32|were afraid|timebant]], because of the difficulty of fulfilling Christ's words. For they said: [[10:26|Who then can be saved?|Quis poterit salvus fieri?]]

paras.t: Insuper recitat Marcus quemadmodum Christus passionem suam prædixit Apostolis, addens se tertia die resurrecturum, et quomodo Jacobus et Joannes ex hoc moti sunt ad petendum a Christo, ut unus eorum ad dexteram, aliusque ad sinistram Christi sederet in gloria ejus. Quæ omnia elucidata sunt in Matthæo, exceptis paucis quæ subsequuntur. Potestis baptismo quo ego baptizor, id est sanguinis proprii perfusione vel tinctione qua ego in passione perfundar, baptizari, hoc est lavari, sanguinem vestrum propter justitiam effundendo? Baptismo quo ego baptizor, baptizabimini re, vel animi præparatione. Jacobus enim sanguinem suum fudit pro Christo, ab Herode decollatus. Joannes vero in pace quievit, sed animo martyr fuit, et multa toleravit pro Christo.
paras.en: Moreover, Mark relates how Christ foretold His passion to the Apostles, adding that He would rise again on the third day, and how James and John were moved by this to ask of Christ that one of them might sit at Christ's right hand and the other at His left in His glory. All of this has been made clear on Matthew[[Matt 20:18||]], except for the few points that follow. [[10:38|Can you drink of the chalice that I drink of or be baptized with the baptism wherewith I am baptized?|Potestis baptismo quo ego baptizor, id est sanguinis proprii perfusione vel tinctione qua ego in passione perfundar, baptizari]], that is, with the pouring out or dyeing of My own blood with which I shall be drenched in the passion, that is, be washed, by shedding your blood for justice' sake? [[10:39|with the baptism wherewith I am baptized you shall be baptized|Baptismo quo ego baptizor, baptizabimini]], in deed, or in readiness of mind. For James shed his blood for Christ, beheaded by Herod[[Acts 12:2||]] [the margin as read gives Act. xii, 9; the death of James is Acts 12:2]. John, however, fell asleep in peace, but he was a martyr in spirit, and bore many things for Christ.

paras.t: Consequenter describitur illuminatio cæci, qui erat filius Timæi, propter quod dicitur Bartimæus, a BAR, quod est filius, et TIMÆUS, quasi filius Timæi. Patetque expositio ex his quæ in Matthæo dicta sunt. In fine autem illius capituli habetur quod erant duo cæci; sed quoniam unus famosior erat, idcirco dumtaxat recitat Marcus de uno.
paras.en: Next is described the enlightening of the blind man, who was [[10:46|the son of Timeus|filius Timæi]], for which reason he is called Bartimeus, from BAR, which is “son”, and TIMÆUS, as though “son of Timeus”. And the exposition is plain from what was said on Matthew[[Matt 20:29||]]. At the end of that chapter, however, we have that there were two blind men[[Matt 20:30||]]; but since one was the better known, Mark tells only of the one.
